content: The larvae in each container are fed with a diet that may consist of protein flakes, commonly used for aquarium fish, or powdered cat biscuits. The containers are maintained at a temperature of 25 ± 2°C. It is critical to ensure that the amount of food provided is minimal to prevent excessive bacterial growth, which can be lethal to the larvae. Feeding should occur several times with intervals of one or two days, and daily observation of the larvae is recommended for optimal care. If the water becomes turbid, all water should be replaced by filtering out the larvae and transferring them to a clean container with fresh water and feed. After five to seven days, a uniform population of early fourth instar larvae, approximately five days old and measuring 4 to 5 mm in length, should be achieved. However, obtaining a homogeneous population of fourth instar larvae is more challenging for Culex pipiens pipiens. To achieve this, a large number of egg rafts must be laid and collected on the same day. These egg rafts can be stored at 15–18°C to accumulate more eggs for hatching. The first instar larvae are delicate and should not be handled. Development to the second instar typically takes 3–4 days at 25 ± 2°C after the eggs are laid. When the larvae reach the second instar stage, they are grouped in a tray containing 3 liters of dechlorinated water at a depth of 4–6 cm, with 800–1000 larvae per tray. Food, such as yeast extract and dog or cat biscuits, is provided as needed. Early fourth instar larvae suitable for testing are usually obtained within seven days, although in some cases, it may take eight or nine days. The maximum acceptable levels of microbial contaminants have not yet been determined. For the fly larvae toxicity test, it is not necessary to conduct a test if the manufacturer has demonstrated that the Bacillus thuringiensis strain does not produce beta-exotoxin. Similarly, no test is required for Bacillus sphaericus as this species is not known to produce exotoxins. The water content of microbial larvicides should generally not exceed 5% to prevent premature degradation of the product. Microbial larvicides should be stored at cool temperatures, but accelerated storage stability tests would be beneficial for quickly assessing the storage stability of products. Currently, no standardized method for such tests exists. In the absence of an accelerated storage stability test, the following minimum standards are recommended: (a) no more than 10% loss in biopotency below the labeled potency value when stored at 5°C for two years, and (b) no more than 10% loss in biopotency below the labeled potency value when stored at 20–25°C for one year. These storage stability tests should be conducted using representative product samples, and biopotency should be assessed using the test method described in Note 4. Results from the biopotency test may vary by up to ±25% from the average, and this variability must be considered when determining potency loss. If oneand two-year test data are not available at the time of drafting a specification, an estimate of storage stability may be acceptable pending completion of the tests. Bacterial larvicide wettable powders (WP) must consist of a homogeneous mixture of the specified bacterial genus, species, subspecies, and strain, along with fillers and other necessary formulants. The formulation should be in the form of a fine powder for dispersion in water, dry, free-flowing, and free from visible extraneous matter and hard lumps. The active ingredient must comply with an identity test and, if necessary, at least one additional test to confirm its identity. The active ingredient content, expressed in International Toxic Units (ITU/mg product), must not be less than 90% of the declared minimum content when determined by the specified method. The material must be free from beta-exotoxin when tested using the fly larvae toxicity test or an equivalent HPLC method. The formulation must also meet specific physical and chemical criteria, such as maximum microbial contamination levels and suspension properties, as outlined in the guidelines. For bioassays, the biopotency of Bacillus thuringiensis subsp. israelensis (Bti) products is compared against a lyophilized reference powder (IPS 82, strain 1884) using early fourth instar larvae of Aedes aegypti (strain Bora Bora). The toxicity of IPS 82 is assigned a value of 15,000 ITU/mg powder against this insect strain. Similarly, the biopotency of Bacillus sphaericus (Bsph) products is determined against a lyophilized reference powder (SPH 88, strain 2362) using early fourth instar larvae of Culex pipiens pipiens (strain Montpellier). The toxicity of SPH 88 is assigned a value of 1,700 ITU/mg powder against this insect strain. Alternative bacterial larvicide reference powders or mosquito strains must be approached cautiously, as different results are inevitable. Cross-calibration against the reference powders and strains should ideally be conducted by independent expert laboratories. The alternative powders/strains and supporting cross-calibration data should be made available to anyone wishing to use or verify the test with these alternatives. For bioassays, reference standard suspensions are prepared by mixing the reference powder with deionized water and a wetting agent, ensuring no foam formation. The suspension is homogenized and checked microscopically for aggregates. Aliquots of the suspension can be stored at 4°C for one month or in a freezer at -18°C for two years. Stock solutions are prepared by diluting the primary suspension to a specific concentration, and subsequent dilutions are made for testing. For products of unknown toxicity, range-finding bioassays are conducted using a wide range of concentrations to determine approximate toxicity. This information is then used to refine the concentration range for a more precise bioassay. Mortality is determined at 24 and 48 hours by counting live larvae, and pupae are excluded from calculations. Tests with control mortality exceeding 5% or pupation greater than 5% are invalidated. Statistical programs, such as SAS, incorporating Log Probit Analysis, are preferred for data analysis to ensure accuracy and eliminate the need for manual corrections. The toxicity of an unknown preparation is determined by comparing the LC50 values of the tested product and reference standard preparations.
